title: Hola at home
hookLine: a sports day, gatka or games in the spirit of Hola Mohalla
tomorrow: Rubi saw a picture of two boys by a wall. what do you tell her?

lines: A FINISH LINE MADE OF A HOSE.
cards: Saturday morning, a backyard, cousins everywhere. Someone is marking a finish line with a garden hose. Someone's uncle is losing badly at tug-of-war.
Two kids are fencing with pool noodles, very seriously, bowing first. It looks like a family field day, and it is. It's also a small nod to a festival a Guru started on purpose.
So, one question for today: can play be holy?

teach.h: HOLA: DRILLS AND SKILL, THE DAY AFTER HOLI.
teach.b: Sikhs answer with Hola Mohalla. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gathered the Sikhs at Anandpur the day after Holi, not for colored powder but for drills, mock battles and contests of skill.
It still runs that way, with gatka, the Sikh art of stick and sword, with horsemanship, kirtan and poetry.
Underneath is the saint-soldier: devotion and strength aren't opposites. A body that can run, stand and protect others belongs to a life given to the Name. And it's done in joy, not in anger.
Now a neighbor, in its own words. In the book of Nehemiah, which Jews and Christians both read, the people gather to hear their law read aloud, and they weep.

They're told to stop grieving and celebrate, and the King James Bible gives the reason: "for the joy of the LORD is your strength." Shared ground: joy isn't a break from faith; strength comes out of it.

teach.h: A FEAST THERE, A TRAINING HERE.
teach.b: In Nehemiah, the joy is a feast: eat, drink, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready.
At Hola, the joy is training: bodies made ready to protect someone else. Two traditions, each in its own way, call gladness holy.

how: Hola Mohalla is held at Anandpur Sahib the day after Holi, with gatka, horsemanship, kirtan and a procession; away from Anandpur, some gurdwaras and families hold gatka displays, sports days or games in its spirit.

s: Hola Mohalla is the Sikh version of Holi, with colored powder
tradition says Guru Gobind Singh made the day after Holi a day of drills, mock battles and skill.
Nehemiah says: for the joy of the LORD is your strength
a neighbor's words: the people stop grieving, feast, and send portions to those with nothing.
in Sikh teaching, devotion and physical strength pull in opposite directions
the saint-soldier holds them together: a body ready to protect, in a life given to the Name.

games.q: a friend says faith should be solemn, so laughing and racing on a holy day is disrespectful. what fits today's lesson?
o: Hola trains strength in joy, and Nehemiah says joy is strength; gladness can be holy.
joy is fine at home, but a holy day itself should stay quiet and serious.
Hola and Nehemiah are the same festival in two languages, so both say the same.
games.why: shared ground: joy as strength. honest difference: Nehemiah's joy is a feast shared with those who have nothing; Hola's is training to protect. two ways, each its own.

practice: Stand up if you can. Roll your shoulders, shake out your hands, then walk slowly around the room, or march gently in place, one step for each breath.
Feel your feet, your legs, your arms: everything that could carry someone if it had to. Keep moving softly until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Hola at home. A family games day, a race, gatka or a tug-of-war, in the spirit of Hola Mohalla: strength trained in joy.

orig.note: Punjabi: the name is explained more than one way; mohalla is often taken as an organized column on the march.

carryVoice: This one goes with you: strength in joy, the saint and the soldier on the same lawn. Day 1756, and dad finally won a race.
